models.inverse_notes: Solve emf given V,I,r: emf=V+I*r, requiring r>=0 and recovered emf>=0; V=13,I=-2,r=0.5 recovers 12 and substitutes to 13. Solve I given emf,V,r: I=(emf-V)/r requires r>0; the same tuple recovers -2 A. r=0,V=emf leaves any current possible, while r=0,V!=emf is inconsistent. Solve r given emf,V,I: r=(emf-V)/I requires I!=0, emf>=0 and recovered r>=0; 12,13,-2 recovers 0.5 ohm. I=0,V=emf leaves every nonnegative r possible; I=0,V!=emf is inconsistent. Recovered r=0 is allowed with nonzero I and V=emf. Each nonsingular inverse has one value; fixed-source applicability remains required.
limitations: No state-of-charge, thermal, ageing or time evolution is predicted. Internal resistance is an effective parameter, not a universal material constant.

models.inverse_notes: With K=N_A fixed, solve z=n*M/(rho_m*K): rho_m>0,M>0,n>=0; the synthetic tuple n=2.408856304e28,rho_m=1200,M=0.06 returns z=2, and n=0 returns z=0. Solve rho_m=n*M/(z*K) requires z>0,M>0 and recovered rho_m>0; the tuple returns 1200. Solve M=z*rho_m*K/n requires n>0,rho_m>0 and recovered M>0; the tuple returns 0.06. All three substitute to the stated n. If z=n=0, rho_m or M is undetermined within its positive domain. If z=0,n>0, no solution. With z>0,n=0, positive finite rho_m,M cannot satisfy the relationship. N_A is not an inverse target. All admissible single-target inverses are unique; z inversion is only population consistency, not a physical carrier-activation theory.
limitations: Mixed constituents require a consistent effective host entity or a sum over constituents; arbitrary averaging of molar masses is not supplied.
No band-structure, ionization or carrier-activation prediction is supplied. Real yield and material-property uncertainty dominate; exact N_A adds no uncertainty.

assumptions: Source calibration population: commercial copper conductors, including physical differences from annealing/hard drawing. Alloy applicability requires evidence; the rule is not asserted for all copper alloys.

Source reports agreement within 0.00001 K^-1 for investigated samples above 94 percent conductivity. An extension for 19 arsenic-bearing cast samples from 30–94 percent reports agreement within 0.0001 K^-1. These are separate qualified populations, not confidence intervals.

At 20 degrees Celsius use the constant-mass/free-expansion resistance coefficient. Source temperature-resistance measurements described on printed p. 4 span 10–100 degrees Celsius; this calibration output is normalized at 20, not a prediction of full nonlinear temperature behavior.

gaps: Add K^-1 and relative_electrical_conductivity with explicit IACS reference basis at 20 degrees Celsius. Reuse resistance_temperature_coefficient only with this normalization and mechanical condition.
Do not bind this fraction to an absolute S/m conductivity or to an arbitrary dimensionless efficiency. Context must verify sample population; no blanket numeric-only acceptance.

models.inverse_notes: Solve f from alpha20: f=alpha20/0.00393. The fixed positive slope has no zero denominator or root branch; recovered f must satisfy f>=0.30 and the same commercial/arsenic population conditions. alpha20=0.00383175 K^-1 returns f=0.975 and substitutes exactly. alpha20=0 gives f=0 outside the calibration; it does not identify zero-conductivity copper. At f=0.30 the model gives 0.001179 K^-1, admissible only for the specified arsenic-bearing extension, not arbitrary alloys. Inferring a conductivity fraction from an empirical coefficient inherits model disagreement and is not statistical or causal invertibility.
limitations: Source does not provide raw calibration data, a probability model, a confidence level or a complete numeric upper commercial-conductivity limit. Scalar f>=0.30 is necessary but not sufficient; population matching is mandatory.

Reference coefficient lists are approximate engineering values. Source observed agreement bounds are historical sample findings, not guaranteed prediction errors. No default conductivity is assigned to an actual specimen.

references.method: Published alpha20=0.00393 K^-1 for 100-percent conductivity retained. A half last printed digit is 0.000005 K^-1; f=1 defines the standard rather than a noisy measurement.

references.method: Oracle independently derived from the prose hard-drawn alpha0=0.00415 K^-1: a linear curve normalized at zero Celsius gives alpha20=alpha0/(1+20*alpha0). This uses reference-resistance renormalization, not the f-to-alpha expression. Half-digit alpha0 uncertainty contributes <4.3e-6; f rounding contributes <2e-6 and rule-slope rounding <4.9e-6, totaling <1.2e-5 K^-1. No table column or garbled alpha20 label is needed.

relationship.original_equation: Faithful prose rule: multiply decimal relative copper conductivity by 0.00393 to obtain the resistance temperature coefficient at 20 degrees Celsius.
relationship.translation_notes: Local f replaces the source decimal conductivity fraction n to avoid collision with carrier density. alpha20 denotes the 20-degree resistance coefficient. f=0.975 means 97.5 percent IACS, not 0.975 percent; input unit is 1. The inlined calibration slope 0.00393 K^-1 is attributed in constants. Celsius and kelvin temperature differences have identical increments. [alpha20]=Theta^-1; coefficient times dimensionless fraction gives K^-1. Clear prose formalizes the relationship; no ambiguous scanned equation or table is transcribed. This calibration estimates a parameter of the prior thermal model; it is a distinct empirical mapping, not a solve direction of that model.

Commercial samples above 94 percent and arsenic-bearing cast samples from 30–94 percent have different reported agreement bounds. Prose supplies the rule; no ambiguous table equation is used.
